A Look at Datastar

04·11·2026

I have always been interested in frontend solutions for building web applications. Even though I’m more of a backend programmer, I really dig all the different techniques people come up with for creating browser-based apps that are both reactive (reflecting remote state in real-time) and interactive (responding to user actions).

Over the last few years, I’ve been looking at different frontend frameworks and libraries, to see how they work, and what I can learn from them. I adore Svelte, which is really smart and efficient. Its sister framework SvelteKit inspired the file-based routing in my own web framework for Ruby, Syntropy. I also really like the approach of the Phoenix framework to building reactive apps using LiveView, which is an amazing technology that builds on the solid concurrency foundation of Elixir/Erlang.

Many people have tried to recreate the same functionality for other languages or frameworks, with varying degrees of success. Recently, Marco Roth came up with ReActionView, which promises to bring reactive views to Rails apps, building on his previous work on Herb, a set of tools that improve on the developer experience of writing ERB templates for Rails apps.

All those different technologies are certainly impressive, but they all are tied to specific languages/frameworks: Svelte/SvelteKit is a JS framework, LiveView is for Phoenix/Elixir, ReActionView is for Ruby on Rails, LiveWire is for Laravel/PHP, etc.

And then there’s Datastar, which dubs itself “the Hypermedia framework”. It is somewhat similar to other frontend declarative frameworks/libraries such as HTMX or Alpine.js, in that interactivity/reactivity is done declaratively by adding attributes to HTML tags. But what is different about Datastar is that it insists on keeping state where it should be, such that it doesn’t try to copy server state to the client and keep it in sync with the server. Instead, the server continuously sends updates (in the form of HTML patches, or signal patches) to the client. In that respect, Datastar is more like LiveView, but without the coupling to Phoenix/Elixir. In fact, Datastar offers SDKs for different languages and frameworks, including Ruby (the Ruby SDK is maintained by Ismael Celis).

I find this approach so refereshing! With Datastar, you can use any backend technology in order to build reactive web apps. Furthermore, Datastar relies on SSE (server-sent events) for streaming updates from the server to the client, instead of the somewhat older approach of using a WebSocket connection used in technologies such as LiveView, or HotWire (the current go-to solution for Rails apps).

While SSE does not provide a full-duplex connection to the server (meaning, you can’t use an SSE request/connection to send data from the client to the server), it provides two important advantages over WebSocket: A WebSocket connection normally requires establishing a separate HTTP/1.1 connection to the server (there’s partial support for WebSocket over HTTP/2, but that depends on the browser and the server/reverse proxy used. HTTP/3 support is very limited as far as I could tell). In contrast, SSE requests can be multiplexed on top of an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection, along with any number of other concurrent requests. Secondly, because SSE requests are just normal (streaming) HTTP requests, the server can use standard HTTP compression in order to achieve significant reduction in bandwidth.

Let’s look at a simple example of working with Datastar. Here’s the markup for a simple reactive app that displays the current time on the server:

<html>
  <head>
    <script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/starfederation/datastar@v1.0.4/bundles/datastar.js">
    </script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p data-init="@get('/ds/time_stream')">
      <span>Time:</span> <span data-text="$time" />
    </p>
  </body>
</html>

This example does three things: load the datastar library (BTW it’s only about 15KB!), set up a connection to an SSE stream at /ds/time_stream using the @get action, and binds a span to a signal named $time. On the server side, the controller looks as follows (using Syntropy):

# /ds/time_stream.rb
export ->(req) {
  req.respond_sse {
    send_time_update(req)
    @machine.periodically(1) { send_time_update(req) }
  }
}

def send_time_update(req)
  json = JSON.dump(time: Time.now.to_s)
  req.send_event('datastar-patch-signals' => "signals #{json}")
end

The controller code is quite simple: after calling respond_sse, which sends some HTTP response headers, we send a first update, then we send further updates once per second. What actually gets sent over the wire looks as follows:

HTTP/1.1 200 
Content-Type: text/event-stream

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:55 +0200" }

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:56 +0200" }

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:57 +0200" }
...

The Datastar wire protocol is based on the SSE response format, where each event contains an (optional) event: entry and one or more data: entries. Distinct events are separated by double newline characters (\n\n). In this case, we’re sending a datastar-patch-signals event that tells the browser to update signal values. The patched values are expressed as a JSON object where the keys correspond to signal names and the values correspond to the signal values.

You can look at this example on a separate page, but for the sake of convenience I’ll go ahead and embed it right here:

Time:

Although this is a very simple example, look at all the things we’re not doing 😜: we don’t need to set up an EventSource object, or use fetch to start the SSE connection on the client side, we don’t need to go through the DOM and update anything that’s bound to the $time signal. On the server side we just stream changes to the server state to the client (eventually though, we might want to introduce some abstractions for sending a datastar-patch-signals event or other types of events, but this is pretty trivial…)

Exploring Signals in Datastar

Let’s look at how signals are handled in Datastar a bit more closely. I’ve been playing with Datastar in the last few days and have observed the some peculiarities:

In Datastar, signals are global to the page. They can’t be scoped to a part of the DOM, but they can be namespaced by nesting them inside objects:

<span data-text:foo.bar.baz />

Alternatively, you can use the following notation, handy when you have key values that contain slashes, or other special characters:

<span data-text="$foo['/bar']" />

By default, Datastar will send all signal values back to the server on every user action, which may be problematic if you have lots of signals on your page. In order to prevent signal values from being sent to the server on each request, the signal name must begin with an underscore.

Finally, an important aspect of Datastar signals (and indeed, Datastar in general,) is that Datastar doesn’t really have a Javascript API. You can’t just access signal values from Javascript (this is by design), which may make it harder to integrate Datastar with other tools. But there is a workaround for that and it’s pretty simple:

<body 
  data-signals="{ foo: { bar: 42 } }"
  data-init="Foo.start($foo);"
>
  <p>foo.bar: <span data-text="$foo.bar" /></p>
  <script>
    window.Foo = {
      start: (foo) => {
        Foo.foo = foo;
        setInterval(() => Foo.foo.bar++, 1000)
      }
      
    };
  </script>
</body>

Here, we use the data-init attribute that lets us run an arbitrary piece of JS. We call Datastar.start, while in a separate <script> we declare a global Datastar object, which stores the reference to the $foo signal, and then sets up a recurring timer to increment the value of $foo.bar once per second:

foo.bar:

This is not too complicated, but then again, a random frontend developer might balk at the fact that Datastar actually makes it hard to access the app state from any other JS library or script on the browser. But I think this makes sense, given the intention behind its design. In “The Tao of Datastar” this is laid out quite explicitly:

State in the right place: Most state should live in the backend… the backend should be the source of truth for your application state…

Use signals sparingly: A good rule of thumb is to only use signals for user interactions (e.g. toggling element visibility) and for sending new state to the backend (e.g. by binding signals to form input elements).

I think constraints are good, and in the case of Datastar, the constraints (no JS API, don’t overuse signals, state should mostly live on the backend), actually make you think hard about the structure of your app, the different pages it’s made of and the components therein. You might even need to rethink the entire URL structure of your app, and where each part of the app state is kept. The more I tinker with Datastar, the more those constraints make sense.

That said, for some types of applications those constraints may be, well, too constraining. For example, an application in which a single page can display thousands of discrete values, and some of them more than once, might need to structure their signals accordingly. In that type of app, we can take advantage of Datastar’s signal namespacing (nested signals) feature, and we might also want to prepend those signals with an underscore, e.g. $_values, so as to prevent all those values from being sent to the server on each request (and anyways the server is the source of those values, so there’s no point in that.)

So if we’re not supposed to use signals for server state, how do we update the client when the server state changes? The answer to that is by patching the page HTML itself:

# /ds/time_stream_html.rb

@time_template = ->(time) {
  span "Time: #{time.to_s}", id: "time"
}

def send_time_update(req)
  patch = Papercraft.html(@time_template, Time.now)
  req.send_event('datastar-patch-elements' => "elements #{patch}")
end

Here we have a micro-template that renders a time span, and we use the datastar-patch-elements event to patch the browser’s DOM. The result works the same as the above example using signals:

Time:

So, this technique of patching the browser DOM requires a somewhat different way of thinking. Most importantly, it requires that the elements that need to be patched be identifiable, normally using an id. This may not necessarily work for all kinds of apps, but in that case you can always use signals. I find that both techniques have their advantages and disadvantages. What’s most interesting though is that with Datastar there’s no need for writing Javascript, and that in itself is a huge advantage.

SPAs vs. MPAs

Datastar is expressly geared more towards creating MPAs (multi-page apps) than SPAs (single-page apps). From the Datastar Tao:

Make an MPA, each page is a resource, keep a stream open on the current state of that resource…

So, is Datastar incompatible with SPAs? And why would we want to make an SPA in the first place? In many web apps there’s going to be some state that pertains to the client (for example, is the sidebar collapsed or not, are menu groups inside the sidebar collapsed or not, etc.), and some state that’s coming from the server. In many web apps, we’d like to retain the client state (the sidebar again), even if we move between different resources in our app. Architecting our app as an SPA may help us achieve this goal of persisting client state, at the possible cost of not being able to correctly handle navigation history.

From my experiments it seems like it’s totally possible to make an SPA using Datastar by filling in the missing parts with some custom Javascript. But why would I want to use Datastar in this way? Maybe there’s something I’m missing? I must admit that at first I had trouble understanding the tao of Datastar. I think my resistance was due to the fact that I’m just used to the “modern” approach of implementing reactive and interactive web UIs using Javascript - responding to user actions, rendering stuff in the client, etc.

But then I listened to a very interesting talk between David Nolen (the creator of ClojureScript) and Ben Croker and Delaney Gilliland (the guys behind Datastar), where David talks about how Datastar was used in building Instabooks, a fast web UI for Quickbooks. This really piqued my curiosity, so I went on the instabooks website and fortunately they have offer a demo that anybody can try. Go and have a look yourself, it’s really cool!

But what’s even cooler is that, as David tells it in their conversation, any user action, such as scrolling records, filtering, searching, etc. results in a full rerendering of the page. I actually looked at what their demo is sending on their SSE stream - it’s always a fully-rendered version of the page. This means that there’s basically (to my understanding) no (or very little) frontend logic that intercepts button clicks and renders a bunch of stuff. Instead, when the UI state is kept on the server, and each interaction results in an HTTP request to the server, which rerenders the page and sends it back to the browser on the previously established SSE stream. For example, when clicking the filter button on a column header, the server will rerender the page, with a little floating filter dialog that’s custom made to the specific column. The updated HTML will be sent to the browser, and Datastar will take care of morphing the DOM to reflect the updated UI state. It works quite beautifully, and it’s fast as well.

What does this way of doing things gets us? First and foremost, we get rid of a lot of frontend Javascript code. As David mentions in the same video, just the thought of having to deal with scrolling, dialogs, live search, etc. is kinda daunting - doing all that stuff in Javascript. Secondly, we can build the entire UI on the server, and have our UI reflect our application state, as in UI = λ(state), just like React! A corollary of this is that testing our app in a way becomes much simpler. Maybe we don’t need the whole Capybara setup to test our app. Instead, since every interaction causes a change of state, we can just test the rendered HTML reflects the state correctly.

The obvious drawback to this way of doing things is that the server now needs to do a lot more work, since it needs to render an entire page’s worth of HTML on each user interaction. For a heavyweight, relatively slow framework such as Rails, this might be a problem. For any app where you need to fetch a bunch of records from a remote database that might be a problem. I imagine that a more fine-grained approach to updating the browser upon user actions with Datastar might work better for those apps where rendering a page is slow. But if your app is built on top of a snappy framework/runtime, and persists its state to e.g. an SQLite database, rerendering the whole page on each interaction may work just fine.

Conclusion

It took me quite a while to understand the Datastar way. At first I really resisted it, and this article in some way reflects this fact - it starts with whole different attitude than how it ends. Believe me when I tell you the first few versions of this article were all about how to work around Datastar’s so-called “limitations”. But now I think I get it, and I can’t wait to start building stuff the Datastar way.

One of the things that were hard for me to understand when I just started looking at Datastar was, how would the backend need to be structured in order to work with Datastar. There was no information about this in the datastar docs, and I felt a bit frustrated because of that. But once things clicked for me I understood this is in fact a non-issue. As the tao of Datastar says:

Make an MPA, each page is a resource…

So the answer is as simple as it gets: build your app normally as a set of resources, render everything on the server. This is such a refreshing approach! In fact, I think I might integrate Datastar into Syntropy and provide additional abstractions that make it easier to build apps using it. With Datastar, there’s a whole new and exciting way of building web apps that’s still waiting to be explored.

blocks.html_en: So, is Datastar incompatible with SPAs? And why would we want to make an SPA in the first place? In many web apps there’s going to be some state that pertains to the client (for example, is the sidebar collapsed or not, are menu groups inside the sidebar collapsed or not, etc.), and some state that’s coming from the server. In many web apps, we’d like to retain the client state (the sidebar again), even if we move between different resources in our app. Architecting our app as an SPA may help us achieve this goal of persisting client state, at the possible cost of not being able to correctly handle navigation history.

This means that there’s basically (to my understanding) no (or very little) frontend logic that intercepts button clicks and renders a bunch of stuff. For a heavyweight, relatively slow framework such as Rails, this might be a problem. For any app where you need to fetch a bunch of records from a remote database that might be a problem. I imagine that a more fine-grained approach to updating the browser upon user actions with Datastar might work better for those apps where rendering a page is slow. But if your app is built on top of a snappy framework/runtime, and persists its state to e.g. an SQLite database, rerendering the whole page on each interaction may work just fine.

content_html_zh:
A Look at Datastar

04·11·2026

I have always been interested in frontend solutions for building web applications. Even though I’m more of a backend programmer, I really dig all the different techniques people come up with for creating browser-based apps that are both reactive (reflecting remote state in real-time) and interactive (responding to user actions).

Over the last few years, I’ve been looking at different frontend frameworks and libraries, to see how they work, and what I can learn from them. I adore Svelte, which is really smart and efficient. Its sister framework SvelteKit inspired the file-based routing in my own web framework for Ruby, Syntropy. I also really like the approach of the Phoenix framework to building reactive apps using LiveView, which is an amazing technology that builds on the solid concurrency foundation of Elixir/Erlang.

Many people have tried to recreate the same functionality for other languages or frameworks, with varying degrees of success. Recently, Marco Roth came up with ReActionView, which promises to bring reactive views to Rails apps, building on his previous work on Herb, a set of tools that improve on the developer experience of writing ERB templates for Rails apps.

All those different technologies are certainly impressive, but they all are tied to specific languages/frameworks: Svelte/SvelteKit is a JS framework, LiveView is for Phoenix/Elixir, ReActionView is for Ruby on Rails, LiveWire is for Laravel/PHP, etc.

And then there’s Datastar, which dubs itself “the Hypermedia framework”. It is somewhat similar to other frontend declarative frameworks/libraries such as HTMX or Alpine.js, in that interactivity/reactivity is done declaratively by adding attributes to HTML tags. But what is different about Datastar is that it insists on keeping state where it should be, such that it doesn’t try to copy server state to the client and keep it in sync with the server. Instead, the server continuously sends updates (in the form of HTML patches, or signal patches) to the client. In that respect, Datastar is more like LiveView, but without the coupling to Phoenix/Elixir. In fact, Datastar offers SDKs for different languages and frameworks, including Ruby (the Ruby SDK is maintained by Ismael Celis).

I find this approach so refereshing! With Datastar, you can use any backend technology in order to build reactive web apps. Furthermore, Datastar relies on SSE (server-sent events) for streaming updates from the server to the client, instead of the somewhat older approach of using a WebSocket connection used in technologies such as LiveView, or HotWire (the current go-to solution for Rails apps).

While SSE does not provide a full-duplex connection to the server (meaning, you can’t use an SSE request/connection to send data from the client to the server), it provides two important advantages over WebSocket: A WebSocket connection normally requires establishing a separate HTTP/1.1 connection to the server (there’s partial support for WebSocket over HTTP/2, but that depends on the browser and the server/reverse proxy used. HTTP/3 support is very limited as far as I could tell). In contrast, SSE requests can be multiplexed on top of an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection, along with any number of other concurrent requests. Secondly, because SSE requests are just normal (streaming) HTTP requests, the server can use standard HTTP compression in order to achieve significant reduction in bandwidth.

Let’s look at a simple example of working with Datastar. Here’s the markup for a simple reactive app that displays the current time on the server:

<html>
  <head>
    <script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/starfederation/datastar@v1.0.4/bundles/datastar.js">
    </script>
  </head>
  <body>
    <p data-init="@get('/ds/time_stream')">
      <span>Time:</span> <span data-text="$time" />
    </p>
  </body>
</html>

This example does three things: load the datastar library (BTW it’s only about 15KB!), set up a connection to an SSE stream at /ds/time_stream using the @get action, and binds a span to a signal named $time. On the server side, the controller looks as follows (using Syntropy):

# /ds/time_stream.rb
export ->(req) {
  req.respond_sse {
    send_time_update(req)
    @machine.periodically(1) { send_time_update(req) }
  }
}

def send_time_update(req)
  json = JSON.dump(time: Time.now.to_s)
  req.send_event('datastar-patch-signals' => "signals #{json}")
end

The controller code is quite simple: after calling respond_sse, which sends some HTTP response headers, we send a first update, then we send further updates once per second. What actually gets sent over the wire looks as follows:

HTTP/1.1 200 
Content-Type: text/event-stream

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:55 +0200" }

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:56 +0200" }

event: datastar-patch-signals
data: signals { "time": "2026-11-04 11:54:57 +0200" }
...

The Datastar wire protocol is based on the SSE response format, where each event contains an (optional) event: entry and one or more data: entries. Distinct events are separated by double newline characters (\n\n). In this case, we’re sending a datastar-patch-signals event that tells the browser to update signal values. The patched values are expressed as a JSON object where the keys correspond to signal names and the values correspond to the signal values.

You can look at this example on a separate page, but for the sake of convenience I’ll go ahead and embed it right here:

Time:

Although this is a very simple example, look at all the things we’re not doing 😜: we don’t need to set up an EventSource object, or use fetch to start the SSE connection on the client side, we don’t need to go through the DOM and update anything that’s bound to the $time signal. On the server side we just stream changes to the server state to the client (eventually though, we might want to introduce some abstractions for sending a datastar-patch-signals event or other types of events, but this is pretty trivial…)

Exploring Signals in Datastar

Let’s look at how signals are handled in Datastar a bit more closely. I’ve been playing with Datastar in the last few days and have observed the some peculiarities:

In Datastar, signals are global to the page. They can’t be scoped to a part of the DOM, but they can be namespaced by nesting them inside objects:

<span data-text:foo.bar.baz />

Alternatively, you can use the following notation, handy when you have key values that contain slashes, or other special characters:

<span data-text="$foo['/bar']" />

By default, Datastar will send all signal values back to the server on every user action, which may be problematic if you have lots of signals on your page. In order to prevent signal values from being sent to the server on each request, the signal name must begin with an underscore.

Finally, an important aspect of Datastar signals (and indeed, Datastar in general,) is that Datastar doesn’t really have a Javascript API. You can’t just access signal values from Javascript (this is by design), which may make it harder to integrate Datastar with other tools. But there is a workaround for that and it’s pretty simple:

<body 
  data-signals="{ foo: { bar: 42 } }"
  data-init="Foo.start($foo);"
>
  <p>foo.bar: <span data-text="$foo.bar" /></p>
  <script>
    window.Foo = {
      start: (foo) => {
        Foo.foo = foo;
        setInterval(() => Foo.foo.bar++, 1000)
      }
      
    };
  </script>
</body>

Here, we use the data-init attribute that lets us run an arbitrary piece of JS. We call Datastar.start, while in a separate <script> we declare a global Datastar object, which stores the reference to the $foo signal, and then sets up a recurring timer to increment the value of $foo.bar once per second:

foo.bar:

This is not too complicated, but then again, a random frontend developer might balk at the fact that Datastar actually makes it hard to access the app state from any other JS library or script on the browser. But I think this makes sense, given the intention behind its design. In “The Tao of Datastar” this is laid out quite explicitly:

State in the right place: Most state should live in the backend… the backend should be the source of truth for your application state… Use signals sparingly: A good rule of thumb is to only use signals for user interactions (e.g. toggling element visibility) and for sending new state to the backend (e.g. by binding signals to form input elements).

I think constraints are good, and in the case of Datastar, the constraints (no JS API, don’t overuse signals, state should mostly live on the backend), actually make you think hard about the structure of your app, the different pages it’s made of and the components therein. You might even need to rethink the entire URL structure of your app, and where each part of the app state is kept. The more I tinker with Datastar, the more those constraints make sense.

That said, for some types of applications those constraints may be, well, too constraining. For example, an application in which a single page can display thousands of discrete values, and some of them more than once, might need to structure their signals accordingly. In that type of app, we can take advantage of Datastar’s signal namespacing (nested signals) feature, and we might also want to prepend those signals with an underscore, e.g. $_values, so as to prevent all those values from being sent to the server on each request (and anyways the server is the source of those values, so there’s no point in that.)

So if we’re not supposed to use signals for server state, how do we update the client when the server state changes? The answer to that is by patching the page HTML itself:

# /ds/time_stream_html.rb

@time_template = ->(time) {
  span "Time: #{time.to_s}", id: "time"
}

def send_time_update(req)
  patch = Papercraft.html(@time_template, Time.now)
  req.send_event('datastar-patch-elements' => "elements #{patch}")
end

Here we have a micro-template that renders a time span, and we use the datastar-patch-elements event to patch the browser’s DOM. The result works the same as the above example using signals:

Time:

So, this technique of patching the browser DOM requires a somewhat different way of thinking. Most importantly, it requires that the elements that need to be patched be identifiable, normally using an id. This may not necessarily work for all kinds of apps, but in that case you can always use signals. I find that both techniques have their advantages and disadvantages. What’s most interesting though is that with Datastar there’s no need for writing Javascript, and that in itself is a huge advantage.

SPAs vs. MPAs

Datastar is expressly geared more towards creating MPAs (multi-page apps) than SPAs (single-page apps). From the Datastar Tao:

Make an MPA, each page is a resource, keep a stream open on the current state of that resource…

So, is Datastar incompatible with SPAs? And why would we want to make an SPA in the first place? In many web apps there’s going to be some state that pertains to the client (for example, is the sidebar collapsed or not, are menu groups inside the sidebar collapsed or not, etc.), and some state that’s coming from the server. In many web apps, we’d like to retain the client state (the sidebar again), even if we move between different resources in our app. Architecting our app as an SPA may help us achieve this goal of persisting client state, at the possible cost of not being able to correctly handle navigation history.

From my experiments it seems like it’s totally possible to make an SPA using Datastar by filling in the missing parts with some custom Javascript. But why would I want to use Datastar in this way? Maybe there’s something I’m missing? I must admit that at first I had trouble understanding the tao of Datastar. I think my resistance was due to the fact that I’m just used to the “modern” approach of implementing reactive and interactive web UIs using Javascript - responding to user actions, rendering stuff in the client, etc.

But then I listened to a very interesting talk between David Nolen (the creator of ClojureScript) and Ben Croker and Delaney Gilliland (the guys behind Datastar), where David talks about how Datastar was used in building Instabooks, a fast web UI for Quickbooks. This really piqued my curiosity, so I went on the instabooks website and fortunately they have offer a demo that anybody can try. Go and have a look yourself, it’s really cool!

But what’s even cooler is that, as David tells it in their conversation, any user action, such as scrolling records, filtering, searching, etc. results in a full rerendering of the page. I actually looked at what their demo is sending on their SSE stream - it’s always a fully-rendered version of the page. This means that there’s basically (to my understanding) no (or very little) frontend logic that intercepts button clicks and renders a bunch of stuff. Instead, when the UI state is kept on the server, and each interaction results in an HTTP request to the server, which rerenders the page and sends it back to the browser on the previously established SSE stream. For example, when clicking the filter button on a column header, the server will rerender the page, with a little floating filter dialog that’s custom made to the specific column. The updated HTML will be sent to the browser, and Datastar will take care of morphing the DOM to reflect the updated UI state. It works quite beautifully, and it’s fast as well.

What does this way of doing things gets us? First and foremost, we get rid of a lot of frontend Javascript code. As David mentions in the same video, just the thought of having to deal with scrolling, dialogs, live search, etc. is kinda daunting - doing all that stuff in Javascript. Secondly, we can build the entire UI on the server, and have our UI reflect our application state, as in UI = λ(state), just like React! A corollary of this is that testing our app in a way becomes much simpler. Maybe we don’t need the whole Capybara setup to test our app. Instead, since every interaction causes a change of state, we can just test the rendered HTML reflects the state correctly.

The obvious drawback to this way of doing things is that the server now needs to do a lot more work, since it needs to render an entire page’s worth of HTML on each user interaction. For a heavyweight, relatively slow framework such as Rails, this might be a problem. For any app where you need to fetch a bunch of records from a remote database that might be a problem. I imagine that a more fine-grained approach to updating the browser upon user actions with Datastar might work better for those apps where rendering a page is slow. But if your app is built on top of a snappy framework/runtime, and persists its state to e.g. an SQLite database, rerendering the whole page on each interaction may work just fine.

结论

It took me quite a while to understand the Datastar way. At first I really resisted it, and this article in some way reflects this fact - it starts with whole different attitude than how it ends. Believe me when I tell you the first few versions of this article were all about how to work around Datastar’s so-called “limitations”. But now I think I get it, and I can’t wait to start building stuff the Datastar way.

One of the things that were hard for me to understand when I just started looking at Datastar was, how would the backend need to be structured in order to work with Datastar. There was no information about this in the datastar docs, and I felt a bit frustrated because of that. But once things clicked for me I understood this is in fact a non-issue. As the tao of Datastar says:

Make an MPA, each page is a resource…

So the answer is as simple as it gets: build your app normally as a set of resources, render everything on the server. This is such a refreshing approach! In fact, I think I might integrate Datastar into Syntropy and provide additional abstractions that make it easier to build apps using it. With Datastar, there’s a whole new and exciting way of building web apps that’s still waiting to be explored.
